overview:
Jericho is shut tight against Israel. The LORD tells Joshua the city is already given and lays out a strange plan. For six days the armed men, seven priests blowing rams’ horns, and the ark go once around the walls while the people keep silent; on the seventh day they go around seven times. At the long blast the people shout, the wall falls flat, and Israel goes straight in. Every living thing is destroyed, the metal goes to the LORD’s treasury, and the city is burned. Rahab and her family are brought out alive, and Joshua lays a curse on anyone who rebuilds Jericho.

Watch the exception. The whole city is declared “accursed” to the LORD, devoted and off limits, and the one household spared belongs to a Canaanite harlot who hid Israel’s messengers. In the next chapter the line runs the other way: a man of Judah takes what was devoted and dies with his house.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. The Talmud credits Joshua, with the account of his death added by Eleazar and Phinehas; many scholars see the book as part of a larger history compiled in the 7th–6th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Joshua’s lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th century BC, drawing on older sources.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Days after the first Passover in the land (5:10), in Israel’s first month west of the Jordan: about 1406 BC by 1 Kings 6:1, or the late 13th century BC on the later date many scholars prefer.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Jericho, the spring-fed oasis town of the lower Jordan valley, a short march from the camp at Gilgal “in the east border of Jericho” (4:19).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Joshua 24:11 recalls that “the men of Jericho fought against you.” 1 Kings 16:34 reports the curse of v. 26 falling on Hiel of Bethel, who lost his firstborn and youngest sons when he rebuilt the city.

hermeneutics:
The Ugaritic epic of Kirta (13th century BC or earlier) has the god El tell King Kirta how to take the city of Udum. He is to wait outside it for six days without shooting arrows at the city or slinging stones at its walls. On the seventh day the king of Udum, kept awake by the noise of his own animals, sends messengers offering silver, gold and horses for peace. A siege counted in six days with a decisive seventh was a known shape for a war story in Canaan. Joshua 6 uses that shape and changes what the seventh day brings: no envoys come out, and the wall falls.

Around 1700 BC the Anatolian king Anitta took the city of Hattusa, destroyed it, sowed its ground with weeds, and declared that if any king after him resettled it, the Storm-god of heaven should strike him. A curse on rebuilding marked a city as given over to defeat for good. Joshua’s oath in v. 26 belongs to that practice, but sets the price inside the rebuilder’s own family, his firstborn at the foundation and his youngest at the gates.

Jericho is Tell es-Sultan, beside the spring. John Garstang (1930–36) found fallen walls and a burned city and dated its end to about 1400 BC. Kathleen Kenyon (1952–58) showed that his walls were far older and dated the burned city to about 1550 BC, leaving little or nothing for Joshua to take; radiocarbon dates on grain from that burn layer (1995) agree with her. Bryant Wood (1990) restudied her pottery and argued again for about 1400 BC. Recent Italian–Palestinian excavations found a smaller Late Bronze town whose upper levels were later cut away. Most archaeologists follow Kenyon’s date, a minority follow Wood, and the site has not settled the question.

breakdown.label: The captain of the LORD’s host by Jericho
The city shut; the LORD’s plan of six days and seven circuits
Day one: priests, trumpets, ark, and a silent army
Days two to six: once around each day
Seventh day: seven circuits; the city declared accursed
The shout, the fallen wall, the city destroyed
Rahab and her household brought out alive
Joshua’s curse on the rebuilder; his fame spreads

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, from the LORD’s command (vv. 2–5) to its fulfillment day by day.

rows.text: Command: six days, then seven circuits and a shout
The seventh day: the wall falls

notes: **Sevens:** “seven” comes 11 times and “seventh” 3 times, 14 in all. The verb “compass” comes 7 times (vv. 3, 4, 7, 11, 14, and twice in v. 15).

**Horns and ark:** the Hebrew for the trumpet, *shofar*, comes 14 times, and the ark is named 10 times in vv. 4–13, then not again. The procession is told as worship, and the soldiers do nothing until the shout.
**Silence and shout:** the verb “shout” comes 7 times, three of them in v. 10, where Joshua forbids it until the day he commands it.
**Rahab breaks in:** both the order to destroy (v. 17) and its carrying out (vv. 21–25) stop to make room for her.

Chapter 6 opens the conquest (6:1–12:24) and stands as its own unit, from Jericho “straitly shut up” (v. 1) to Joshua’s fame “noised throughout all the country” (v. 27). It closes the Rahab story of ch. 2: the household gathered under the scarlet line in 2:18–19 is the one brought out in vv. 22–23. Many readers join 5:13–15 to it, since the captain of the LORD’s host appears “by Jericho” just before the LORD speaks in v. 2.
**Forward:** the warning of v. 18 that taking the devoted thing would “trouble” the camp uses the verb that names the valley of Achor in 7:25–26.

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to v. 20, where the wall falls, points to a parable given to the Saints driven from Jackson County. The lord of the vineyard commands his servants to “break down the walls of mine enemies” and throw down their tower. It is a thematic link: the Jericho image is applied to the redemption of Zion.

Before storming the walled town of Caspis, Judas Maccabeus and his men call on the great Lord of the world, the one “who without rams or engines of war did cast down Jericho.” The chapter had become a prayer for besiegers. Judas still assaults the walls himself, and takes the town.

A one-page anthology from Cave 4 lists proof texts for the end of days: the prophet like Moses, Balaam’s star, Levi’s blessing, and, last, Joshua’s curse from v. 26. It then expounds the curse with a passage from the Psalms of Joshua about an accursed man of Belial and two instruments of violence who rebuild a city and shed blood. Scholars read it as an attack on a builder of their own day, often a Hasmonean ruler.

Josephus keeps the six days and seven circuits but adds a pause: after the seventh circuit the army “had stood still a little” before the wall fell, with no instrument of war applied. He says Joshua gave Rahab lands at once and held her in great esteem ever after. On the curse he promises to tell later what came of it.

This retelling names the two spies: Kenaz and Seenamias, sons of Caleb, sent because their father had been a faithful spy before them. Then the whole conquest of Jericho shrinks to one sentence: the people besieged the city and burned it with fire. Rahab, the trumpets and the falling wall are all left out.

This early rabbinic chronicle dates the events: Israel crossed the Jordan on the tenth of Nisan, kept Passover on the fourteenth, and began circling Jericho on the twenty-second. Rabbi Yose adds that the day of battle, the seventh, was a Sabbath. Rashi builds on this: the war was lawful that day because God commanded it, and the city was made “accursed,” holy to the LORD, because the spoil was taken on a holy day.
traditions.cite: Seder Olam Rabbah 11; Rashi on Joshua 6:15, 17

traditions.text: The Aramaic translation fills in v. 1: Jericho was shut with doors of iron and bars of bronze, and no one went out to make war or came in to ask after anyone’s welfare. In v. 5 it renders the wall’s fall as being “swallowed up in its place,” the reading the Talmud also knows (next entry).

The Mishnah says that whoever sees a place where miracles were done for Israel blesses God who did miracles for the fathers there. The Talmud’s list of such places includes the crossings of the Jordan, the hailstones at Beth-horon, and “the wall of Jericho that was swallowed.” The detail comes from v. 5, where the wall falls, literally, “under itself”: it sank where it stood rather than toppling outward.

A baraita widens Joshua’s curse: no one may build Jericho under another name, nor give Jericho’s name to another city. Hiel, the Talmud says, buried all his sons one by one from the firstborn to the youngest and should have read the warning in the first death. Elijah and King Ahab visit his house of mourning, and Ahab scoffs that if Moses’ curse of drought has not come, Joshua’s should not either; Elijah answers with the drought of 1 Kings 17:1.

The great chapter on faith gives Jericho one line: “By faith the walls of Jericho fell down,” after seven days of circling. The faith meant is an army’s willingness to march around a wall for a week with nothing to show for it until the seventh day. Rahab follows in the next verse (see chapter 2).

Origen reads Jericho as the world, which will end not by sword or battering ram but at the sound of a trumpet, as Paul says the last day will come. Only the harlot and her household are spared, and he takes Rahab as a figure of the Church and her scarlet cord as a sign of salvation by Christ’s blood. Since Joshua’s name in Greek is Jesus, Origen speaks of the Lord Jesus taking Jericho.
